rationale: A wins because it keeps the best story bounded to the facts: "Glossier's wholesale channel is now growing faster than the DTC business it was built on" is sharp, sourced, and immediately asks what "fastest-growing" means. B keeps inflating the same fact into conclusions it cannot carry: "after a decade of treating retail as the enemy" is not in the update, and "That's a verdict, not a news item" turns one private-company claim into a market obituary. A gives the founder four usable lanes; B gives them one good lane and two headlines that need legal and strategic deflation before a reporter sees them.
gaps_in_A: "LVMH's specialty-retail strategy" imports corporate context not supplied in the update; if this is source-bound, that belongs in proof, not the pitch shape.
"suburban strip-mall retail" and "suburban America" over-read Sephora at Kohl's without demographic or geography evidence.
"one of the few brands with a clean twelve-year arc" is an unsourced rarity claim; the update only supports the 2014 blog origin and current wholesale expansion.
gaps_in_B: "after a decade of treating retail as the enemy" invents hostility. The update says DTC-only, not anti-retail.
"The brand that built the DTC playbook" is outside-knowledge framing, and "That's a verdict, not a news item" overstates one company claim into a category conclusion.
"whether the DTC experiment in prestige beauty is closing out" is a fake trend unless backed by comparative market evidence, which the update does not provide.
The first two angles are padded siblings: both are the DTC-to-wholesale reversal with a different hat, not two genuinely separate pitch lanes.
